record.original_question: For ultra-bright Type II supernovae, how bright can the brightest events be, what physical class are they, and why do they occur; in particular, can pair-annihilation explosions of ultramassive stars above about 140 solar masses and extremely low metallicity below about one-thousandth solar metallicity explain such events in the local universe after more than 13 billion years of chemical evolution?

evidence.quote: At the other end of the scale, it is clear that exceptionally bright SNII do occur, starting with “my" first SN, 1979C, which at maximum was at least as bright as a SNIa (MB < −19.5) [1], to the very recent SN 2005ap [19] and 2006gy [20].
These events pose a number of question, such as “How bright can “ultra-bright" SNe be?", “What are they?", “Why do they occur?", etc.
One of the “simple" suggestions is that they are the result of a pair-annihilation event which is predicted for ultramassive stars (M> 140M⊙) of extremely low metallicities (Z< 1/1000Z⊙).

This is an interesting possibility that is worth considering and pursuing, but I find it hard to imagine that such stars may exist in the local Universe, after more than 13 billion years of chemical evolution.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider Type II supernovae with peak absolute B-band magnitudes brighter than M_B ≈ −19.5 (i.e. comparable to or exceeding typical Type Ia supernovae), such as the class of "ultra-bright" core-collapse events. Address the following questions:

(a) What is the maximum possible peak luminosity (or absolute magnitude) attainable by such ultra-bright Type II supernovae?

(b) What is the physical class and explosion mechanism responsible for these extreme events?

(c) Why do such events occur, i.e. what stellar progenitor configurations and evolutionary pathways lead to them?

(d) In particular, evaluate whether the pair-instability (pair-annihilation) explosion mechanism — predicted for ultramassive stars with zero-age main-sequence mass M > 140 M_⊙ and extremely low metallicity Z < 10^(−3) Z_⊙ — can plausibly account for ultra-bright Type II events observed in the local Universe today, given that more than 1.3 × 10^10 years of cosmic chemical evolution have elapsed and such low-metallicity ultramassive progenitors are not obviously expected to still form locally.
artifact.status_search_result: Subsequent observational and theoretical work has provided partial answers. Several superluminous supernovae (e.g., SN 2007bi) have been proposed as pair-instability candidates, and pulsational pair-instability has been advanced as an alternative for many ultra-bright events (Woosley et al., Nature 2007). However, SN 2006gy was found to have occurred at roughly solar metallicity, inconsistent with the canonical Z < 10^(−3) Z_⊙ requirement, and a 2020 study reinterpreted SN 2006gy as a Type Ia interacting with a dense shell. Thus the maximum luminosity, dominant mechanism, and viability of low-metallicity pair-instability progenitors in the local Universe remain partially resolved and actively debated.

status_evidence.title: Pulsational pair instability as an explanation for the most luminous supernovae
status_evidence.snippet: Pulsational pair instability proposed as a mechanism for the brightest supernovae without requiring extremely low metallicity.
status_evidence.claim: Alternative pair-instability variants can power ultra-bright events, partially answering the mechanism question.

status_evidence.title: A type Ia supernova at the heart of superluminous transient SN 2006gy
status_evidence.snippet: SN 2006gy reinterpreted as a Type Ia supernova interacting with a dense circumstellar shell.
status_evidence.claim: At least one canonical ultra-bright event has been re-explained without invoking pair-instability of an ultramassive low-metallicity star.

status_evidence.title: Pair-instability supernovae in the local universe
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses pair-instability supernova candidates and light-curve modeling at low redshift.
status_evidence.claim: Pair-instability progenitors in the local Universe remain a candidate but observational identification is still uncertain.

status_evidence.title: Possible Detection of a Pair Instability Supernova in the Modern Universe
status_evidence.snippet: Reports candidate pair-instability supernova detection in the modern Universe.
status_evidence.claim: Some evidence supports that pair-instability events may occur locally, though confirmation is incomplete.
